headlines.article_text: Stock market today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, US, Nov. 18, 2026. Brendan McDermid | Reuters U.S. equity futures jumped early Thursday as investors looked ahead to Anthropic's public trading debut. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.38%. S&P 500 futures added 0.59%, and Nasdaq-100 futures surged 0.99% In Asia, markets were mostly lower. South Korea's Kospi fell 0.25% as markets opened an hour later than usual due to the country's annual college entrance exam . Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell 1.89%, while mainland China's CSI 300 declined 0.49%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 closed 1.08% lower. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.48%, while the Topix fell 0.15%. In Wednesday's regular U.S. trading, the blue-chip Dow lost more than 560 points, or 1.1%. The broad market S&P 500 fell 0.2%, marking its fifth consecutive losing session and longest slide since June. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4%. Traders are focused on how the company behind Claude performs when it debuts on the Nasdaq Thursday, trading under the ticker "ANT." The artificial intelligence company priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the expected range, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC Wednesday. Anthropic also upsized the offering, selling around 980 million shares, bringing the amount raised to $81.3 billion and surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June. The market has become more cautious on AI as of late, with investors focusing on whether heavy spending on the build-out will translate into meaningful profits. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) has fallen 11% this month, and embattled AI bellwether Nvidia has dropped 26% while the company grapples with the resignation of its CEO Jensen Huang. Shares of neocloud CoreWeave , which had seen its bond yields trade above 16% earlier this month, is also down almost 13% in November alone. "It'll be an important barometer for investors' AI appetite," Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp, said of Anthropic's IPO. "AI stocks desperately need some wind at their backs, too ... Wall Street needs a sign that investors still believe in the potential for AI beyond already-elevated expectations." "The challenge in that thesis is that hot IPOs rarely perform well right out of the gate, especially these days, when every company seems to be vying for a limited pool of capital to fund their AI strategy," she said. "While I wouldn't be surprised to see the stock market take cues from Anthropic's performance, I'd caution investors about trying to read the tea leaves from one event too much." On Thursday, traders will keep an eye out for weekly jobless claims. On the earnings front, Walmart is slated to report in the morning, followed by clothing retailer Gap after the market close.

Travis Dove | Bloomberg | Getty Images Walmart is scheduled to report its third fiscal quarter earnings Thursday as the retailer prepares for the holiday season with an increased emphasis on value amid lower consumer sentiment. The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership. Here's what the company is expected to report for its fiscal third quarter, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 64 cents expected Revenue: $187.27 billion expected Walmart previously said it expects third-quarter net sales to climb 3% to 3.75%. CFO John David Rainey told CNBC last quarter that Walmart's "business is strong" and that he's encouraged by its progress. The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef. It also saw a significant boost from tariff refunds, which Rainey said Walmart would use to cut prices. In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with its club subsidiary, Sam's Club, as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer standalone memberships. The retailer is also rolling out technology in its stores to improve the customer experience, including light-up digital shelf labels that are connected to its app. Those shelf labels and Walmart's AI push have also sparked concerns that the retailer could try to change prices based on demand and shoppers' personal data, which Walmart has denied. Analysts from UBS wrote in a note last week that they believe the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results will show healthy market share gains. "E-commerce continues to scale, the company's higher-margin alternative revenue streams continue to grow and Walmart is increasingly able to fund investments in price and convenience while still producing attractive operating income growth," the analysts wrote. They added that they expect Walmart's fourth-quarter outlook to include "robust operating income growth." Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year-to-date.
